Frozen originals supply level and complete task structure. No independent teacher or learner calibration, official CET provenance, release or production approval is claimed.

units.title: 四级阅读：洞穴展示图与菜单里的借词
units.instruction: Read both complete passages and choose the best answer to each question using the passage it accompanies.

materials.title: The Passage That Looked Short
materials.text:
A visitor centre displayed a map of an explored cave. The first version showed the route from the entrance to an underground chamber as a short line. Visitors often asked why the guided tour took so long when the chamber appeared so close.

The map showed the cave from above. It was useful for showing which passages connected, but it did not show every rise, descent or narrow section. Two places near each other in that view could be separated by a considerable change in height. Walking along the actual route also required following bends rather than travelling directly through rock.

A volunteer proposed drawing the route to make it look as long as the tour felt. The guide rejected that solution. Deliberately stretching one part would introduce another misunderstanding unless the change was explained. The problem was not that the map was useless; it was being asked to communicate dimensions and effort that its chosen view did not represent.

The centre added a side-view diagram and a short description of the guided visit. The description identified places where the group paused for explanation. Tour duration included those stops as well as movement. The map and the timetable now answered related but distinct questions.

The centre tested the display with people unfamiliar with the cave. Some still preferred the original overhead map for tracing connections. Others found the side view essential for understanding why an apparently nearby chamber was not reached by a simple level walk. Neither image replaced the other.

The revised display was educational rather than a guide for independent exploration. It explained the supplied tour instead of implying that a simplified line contained every condition underground. Visitors could understand what each representation included and what it left out. The centre had improved the explanation by adding a complementary view, not by pretending that one drawing could be a complete copy of a three-dimensional place.

questions.prompt: Why did the original map lead to questions about tour length?
options: It displayed a short overhead route without its full height changes or stops.
It showed a different cave on another coast.
The chamber had been removed from the tour.
The timetable described only the journey to the visitor centre.
questions.explanation: A俯视短线漏高差与讲解停留；B非别洞；C仍在游程；D表述洞内游程。

questions.prompt: Why reject stretching the route without explanation?
options: A map can never use a different scale.
The tour was required to become shorter.
It could replace one misunderstanding with another.
Visitors were forbidden to compare drawings.
questions.explanation: C未标变形会再误导；A不是禁所有比例变化；B未改游程；D鼓励比较。

questions.prompt: What did the side-view diagram add?
options: The names of every visitor.
Information about vertical relationships.
A guarantee that walking effort was identical for everyone.
Permission to explore without a guide.
questions.explanation: B侧面展高低关系；A无访客名单；C未统一体力；D明确非独自探索指南。

questions.prompt: Why did tour duration exceed movement time alone?
options: Every visitor took a different route.
The map had no entrance.
The chamber could be reached only by train.
The group also paused for explanations.
questions.explanation: D包括讲解停顿；A跟统一导览；B有入口；C无火车。

questions.prompt: What principle underlies the revised display?
options: A representation should make its selected dimensions and limits understandable.
An overhead map is always less accurate than a side view.
Adding a timetable makes diagrams unnecessary.
A drawing must reproduce every physical detail to be useful.
questions.explanation: A解释各图选择与限度；B两图互补非上下高低优劣；C仍需图；D简化亦有用。

materials.title: The Dish behind the Borrowed Name
materials.text:
A campus newspaper asked why a neighbourhood restaurant used a foreign word for a dish that differed from the version described in a travel guide. One writer suggested exposing the restaurant as mistaken. The food editor instead asked the cook how the dish had developed.

The cook's family had moved between regions, carrying the name and a basic cooking method with them. Some ingredients had been unavailable in their new home. Others were replaced because customers preferred a different texture. The name had remained, although the plate had changed.

The editor distinguished two possible claims. The restaurant might be promising an exact reproduction of one regional preparation, or it might be using a familiar inherited name for a local version. Those claims should be judged differently. A borrowed word did not by itself tell readers which promise was being made.

The resulting article described the family's route and the changes in ingredients. It also explained what the travel guide meant by the dish in its own regional context. Readers could compare the preparations without being told that only one family's food experience counted as real.

This did not mean every label was beyond criticism. If an ingredient important for dietary restrictions was missing from the explanation, or if an advertisement made a specific inaccurate claim, a history of adaptation would not excuse it. The newspaper kept practical information about the actual plate clear.

Some readers still preferred the travel-guide version. Others wanted to try the restaurant's variation. Their preferences no longer depended on a simple choice between perfect authenticity and complete error. The article showed how a name could travel while a recipe changed, and how useful description could identify the relationship.

The editor's task was not to award ownership of the word. It was to help readers understand what was served, which tradition was being invoked and what had happened along the way. Asking about that history produced a more informative story than correcting a name from a single outside definition.

questions.prompt: What did the editor do before judging the name?
options: Ordered the restaurant to change its menu.
Asked the cook about the dish’s development.
Assumed the travel guide described every possible version.
Deleted all discussion of ingredients.
questions.explanation: B先问来历；A未强令改名；C未视单定义为全部；D实际写食材变化。

questions.prompt: Why had the dish changed?
options: The family had forgotten every cooking method.
The name had never been used before.
The travel guide required local restaurants to alter it.
Ingredient availability and customer preferences differed.
questions.explanation: D材料供应与口味促适应；A保留基本方法；B名称继承；C指南未指挥餐厅。

questions.prompt: Which distinction mattered for assessing the label?
options: A promise of exact regional reproduction versus a name for a local adaptation.
The number of letters in the foreign word.
Whether the cook had ever read a newspaper.
Whether every reader liked the same texture.
questions.explanation: A先辨标签承诺；B拼字长度、C看报经历无关；D不要求人人同好。

questions.prompt: What limit did the article place on the adaptation argument?
options: It prohibited explaining any ingredient changes.
It required every dish to match a guidebook.
It did not excuse inaccurate practical information or explicit claims.
It made dietary information unnecessary.
questions.explanation: C适应史不能免责误导；A写明改料；B非强制单版；D饮食限制更应清楚。

questions.prompt: What was gained by the final approach?
options: A legal award of ownership over the word.
A richer account of what was served and its historical relationship to other versions.
Agreement that all readers should prefer the same dish.
Proof that all menu descriptions are equally precise.
questions.explanation: B说明成菜及传统关系更丰富；A无词权裁决；C保留偏好；D不否认信息需精准。

units.title: 四级阅读：苔藓的绿色地毯与折椅的锁定
units.instruction: Read both complete passages and choose the best answer to each question using the passage it accompanies.

materials.title: A Green Surface That Was Not a Lawn
materials.text:
After a shaded corner of a college garden became covered in moss, a grounds volunteer proposed treating it exactly like the nearby lawn. It looked like another low green carpet, so the same mowing and watering schedule seemed reasonable.

The gardener explained that the resemblance was limited. The moss did not have the same structures as grass. Its small leaf-like parts and surfaces interacted with water differently, and it lacked the same system of true roots. A routine designed for one kind of plant should not be copied merely because another occupied a similar visual role.

The shaded corner also had different conditions from the open lawn. Less direct sunlight reached it, and water remained on the surface longer after rain. The gardener first considered those conditions rather than treating the moss as proof of a single soil problem. Several factors could make a site suitable, and the green covering alone did not identify all of them.

The college decided to retain part of the moss for observation. A low border directed visitors around it because repeated footsteps damaged the delicate growth. The nearby lawn remained available for sitting. The arrangement recognised two uses instead of requiring every green area to support the same activity.

Students watched the moss become duller during a dry period and greener after rain. The gardener cautioned against using colour alone to diagnose its condition. The observations were useful, but understanding growth required attention to time and moisture as well as appearance.

For the display label, the class avoided calling the moss miniature grass. That phrase might help a visitor notice its low form, but it would imply too much similarity. The completed label described both the familiar appearance and the important differences.

The exercise changed how volunteers approached maintenance. They began by asking what organism and conditions they were dealing with, then chose an appropriate routine. A familiar visual category could begin an observation without being a sufficient guide to care.

questions.prompt: Why was the lawn routine initially proposed?
options: The volunteer had measured identical root systems.
Both areas looked like low green carpets.
The shaded corner received more direct sun.
Moss had already been mown successfully for years.
questions.explanation: B相似外观促套流程；A根系不同；C阴处少日；D未有多年成功记录。

questions.prompt: What did the gardener emphasise?
options: Moss and grass differed in structure and water relations.
All green plants needed identical treatment.
Moss colour identified every soil problem.
Grass had no true roots.
questions.explanation: A结构及与水关系异；B反论点；C颜色不足诊断；D无此说法。

questions.prompt: Why was a border added?
options: To make moss grow taller than grass.
To prevent all rain reaching the corner.
To reduce damaging footsteps while preserving an observation area.
To turn the whole lawn into a laboratory building.
questions.explanation: C引流脚步保护观察区；A不增高；B仍雨淋；D草坪仍坐用。

questions.prompt: What caution accompanied the colour observations?
options: They proved no observation was useful.
Dryness could never affect moss appearance.
Every brown patch meant the same disease.
Colour alone was not a complete diagnosis of condition.
questions.explanation: D颜色仅线索；A观测有用；B旱后变暗；C未把暗色定病。

questions.prompt: What broader lesson did volunteers learn?
options: Identify the organism and conditions before copying a maintenance routine.
Replace every unfamiliar plant with grass.
Keep visitors away from all garden surfaces.
Treat visual similarity as proof of biological identity.
questions.explanation: A先识物与环境再选维护；B保留苔；C只部分绕行；D恰否认相似即同类。

materials.title: The Click before Sitting Down
materials.text:
A product-design class examined a folding chair. Open, it resembled an ordinary chair. Folded, its legs moved close together so it could be carried. The students first focused on how smoothly the joints allowed this change.

A technician asked them to identify what prevented the chair from folding while someone sat on it. A support bar had to reach its intended position before a locking part engaged. Smooth movement during opening was not evidence that this final condition had been achieved.

The prototype made a clicking sound near the end of the opening movement. Several testers assumed the sound confirmed that the chair was locked. Inspection showed that a decorative cover could also click when pressed. The same kind of sound could therefore arise before the supporting mechanism was secure.

The class redesigned the cover and added a visible indicator directly connected to the lock. The indicator did not replace mechanical strength. It helped the user recognise a condition that the mechanism itself still had to maintain. The team tested opening, checking and folding as a sequence rather than assessing each isolated feature.

A clear instruction was also supplied. However, the designer argued that a warning label should not carry the whole burden of compensating for a misleading product cue. Users had learned from many objects to interpret a click as completion. The prototype's behaviour encouraged that expectation.

The revised chair was evaluated under the class's supervised testing arrangements. The exercise did not establish a general certification for public use. It taught the students to distinguish ease of motion, a signal of completion and structural support.

An object could feel pleasant to open while communicating the wrong state. Useful feedback needed a dependable relationship to what it appeared to confirm. Improving the chair meant considering that relationship alongside the shape of the seat and the smoothness of its hinges.

questions.prompt: What condition concerned the technician?
options: Whether the chair could be painted in one colour.
Whether every joint moved without sound.
Whether the support and lock prevented unintended folding.
Whether the chair looked ordinary when folded.
questions.explanation: C实际支撑锁定防折；A色彩、B完全无声非重点；D折起并不普通椅外观。

questions.prompt: Why was the original click misleading?
options: It could come from a cover before the lock was secure.
It always occurred only after a certified load test.
The chair could not produce any other sound.
Every tester knew it came from the decorative part.
questions.explanation: A罩件能提前响；B没有认证；C无唯一声源假设；D测试者误认。

questions.prompt: What role did the new indicator serve?
options: It supplied all the chair’s structural strength.
It removed the need for the lock.
It certified public use automatically.
It communicated a state through a direct connection to the lock.
questions.explanation: D与锁联动反映状态；A不承全力；B仍需锁；C未认证。

questions.prompt: Why was an instruction alone insufficient?
options: Reading was prohibited during testing.
The object itself encouraged a misleading expectation.
The class wanted no communication with users.
A chair could not carry a label.
questions.explanation: B产品反馈本身误导，标签不能全补；A可读；C加指标指引；D可贴标签。

questions.prompt: Which distinction did the exercise teach?
options: An object’s colour is the same as its strength.
Smooth movement, completion signals and support are separate design questions.
Every click proves a product is safe.
User expectations can never be influenced by design.
questions.explanation: B动作顺、信号、支撑需分别并关联考量；A色非强度；C响非安全保证；D设计正影响期待。

units.title: 四级阅读：合唱的共同元音与抽奖规则
units.instruction: Read both complete passages and choose the best answer to each question using the passage it accompanies.

materials.title: A Shared Sound without a Shared Accent
materials.text:
A university choir included singers from several regions. During one song, a long vowel sounded blurred even though everyone sang the correct note. The conductor heard small differences in the vowel shapes, which became especially noticeable when the sound was sustained.

One singer suggested that the choir should remove all regional accents. The conductor asked for a narrower goal. The group needed a coordinated vowel for this phrase, not a judgement that one singer's ordinary speech was defective. A pronunciation useful for a sung line could differ from the same word in conversation.

The conductor demonstrated a chosen sound and asked the singers to listen to how it blended. They practised moving into the vowel together and leaving it at the same moment. Pitch remained important, but matching the note alone did not control the character or timing of the sound.

For a later folk song, the group discussed a different decision. Regional pronunciation formed part of the version they were performing, so copying the earlier vowel without considering the new piece would erase a relevant feature. The choir consulted a speaker familiar with that version and recorded the agreed choices.

The rehearsal notes therefore identified the song and phrase rather than declaring a universal correct accent for the choir. New members could understand which choices belonged to a performance and which remained part of individual speech.

Several singers found this approach reassuring. They could work precisely on ensemble sound without feeling that their own voices had to be culturally neutral. The conductor also gained a clearer way to explain corrections. A request to coordinate one sound carried a different meaning from telling someone to speak properly.

The exercise showed that common practice need not require denying difference. A group can agree on a local performance choice while recognising that other choices are appropriate elsewhere. The useful question was what the particular music needed and how the singers could make that intention audible together.

questions.prompt: What caused the blurred sustained sound?
options: Every singer chose a different musical note.
Small vowel differences became noticeable during the long note.
The choir had no regional variety.
The conductor stopped the song before anyone sang.
questions.explanation: B长音暴露元音差异；A音高正确；C成员来自多地区；D已听到唱声。

questions.prompt: What was the conductor’s narrower goal?
options: To prove one regional accent was defective.
To change every singer’s everyday conversation.
To coordinate a vowel for a particular musical phrase.
To replace the song with a speech lesson.
questions.explanation: C局部演唱协调；A非贬口音；B不改所有日常语言；D仍练歌曲。

questions.prompt: Why not copy the first vowel choice into the later folk song automatically?
options: Regional pronunciation could be significant in that version.
The later song contained no words.
The choir had decided never to take advice.
All songs demanded identical pronunciation.
questions.explanation: A地域发音是后曲特征；B有歌词发音；C咨询熟悉者；D不同曲需不同判断。

questions.prompt: Why did the notes specify songs and phrases?
options: To rank singers by the prestige of their birthplace.
To prevent new members understanding the choices.
To label every alternative accent incorrect.
To locate the pronunciation choices within their performance context.
questions.explanation: D标适用上下文；A不排籍贯；B帮助新人；C不宣布普遍唯一正音。

questions.prompt: What principle does the passage illustrate?
options: Ensemble precision requires culturally neutral voices.
Individual differences make collective work impossible.
A shared local practice can coexist with respect for other appropriate choices.
Musical pitch is irrelevant whenever singers share a vowel.
questions.explanation: C共同局部选择与差异共存；A无需文化中性；B合作成功；D音高仍重要。

materials.title: One Prize, Two Different Procedures
materials.text:
A student society sold numbered tickets for a raffle with two prizes. Its draft announcement said that every ticket would have two chances. The treasurer asked the organisers to explain exactly how the draws would work before publishing that phrase.

In the first proposed procedure, the winning ticket from the first draw would be returned to the container before the second draw. The same ticket could then win again. In the second procedure, it would remain outside, so the two winning tickets had to differ. Both involved two draws, but they did not create identical possibilities.

Some organisers thought returning the ticket was unfair because one person might receive both prizes. Others preferred equal treatment of tickets at the start of each draw. These were different ideas about a fair arrangement, not simply competing estimates of how many tickets had been sold.

The society chose to remove the first winning ticket. It still had to decide whether someone holding several tickets could win both prizes through two different numbers. Removing one ticket did not automatically limit prizes to one per person. A rule about numbers and a rule about people were not the same.

The final notice stated both decisions. It also explained that purchasing more tickets increased a person's entries but guaranteed no prize. A volunteer's phrase almost certain was removed because the society had not calculated any basis for that claim.

At the event, the organiser showed the first winning ticket being placed aside. The visible procedure matched the announced rule, so participants did not have to guess whether the ticket had been returned.

The exercise taught the society that a short friendly announcement could hide important choices. Explaining the process did not eliminate every disagreement about fairness. It enabled participants to understand the arrangement before deciding to buy tickets and allowed the actual draw to be checked against a clear description.

questions.prompt: Why did the treasurer question two chances?
options: The phrase did not specify how the two draws related.
The society had announced only one prize.
All tickets had identical numbers.
The container was known to be empty.
questions.explanation: A未解释是否放回，两次机会含糊；B有两奖；C号码不同；D有售票。

questions.prompt: What follows if the first winning ticket is returned?
options: Two different people must win.
The second prize disappears.
The same ticket can be selected again.
Every ticket is guaranteed a prize.
questions.explanation: C放回可同票再中；A不保证两人；B仍两奖；D不是保底。

questions.prompt: What remained undecided after choosing removal?
options: The colour of the container alone.
Whether a person with several tickets could win through two numbers.
Whether a removed ticket could physically return by itself.
Whether numbered tickets existed.
questions.explanation: B一票排除不等一人一奖；A非剩余规则；C不讨论自行回票；D已售编号票。

questions.prompt: Why remove almost certain from the notice?
options: It was longer than the prize names.
The society wanted nobody to understand probability.
Every buyer was in fact certain to win.
There was no calculated support for the claim.
questions.explanation: D未有依据的高概率承诺删除；A非字长；B更清楚信息；C明确不保证。

questions.prompt: What did a clear procedure provide?
options: A guarantee that everyone agreed on fairness.
An arrangement people could understand beforehand and check during the draw.
A way to make two prizes cover every ticket.
Proof that one definition of fairness applied to all raffles.
questions.explanation: B知情选择和现场核验；A仍可分歧；C奖不扩张；D不定所有抽奖唯一公平。

units.title: 四级阅读：书后索引的入口与树牌上的季节
units.instruction: Read both complete passages and choose the best answer to each question using the passage it accompanies.

materials.title: The Name That Led to No Page
materials.text:
A student preparing an index for a local-history book began by collecting every important-looking word. She linked each word to a page where it occurred. The first version seemed thorough because it contained a long list of names and places.

Readers trying the index encountered a problem. They searched for the ferry service, but the book usually discussed it under the harbour company that operated it. The word ferry appeared only occasionally, so the student's method missed several substantial passages. A useful entry needed to follow a topic, not merely reproduce a word search.

The editor also distinguished an index from a table of contents. Chapter headings showed the book's main sequence. An index offered alternative entrances across that sequence, allowing someone interested in work, transport or family life to reach material distributed among several chapters.

The student added a ferry-service entry covering the relevant discussion. A cross-reference directed readers from the company's earlier name to its later one. She did not duplicate every entry without explanation, since readers needed to understand when two labels referred to the same subject.

A second test revealed another issue. Some pages mentioned a person only in a list, while others discussed that person's role at length. The student kept selected brief references where useful but gave priority to pages with substantial information. She also checked page numbers after the final layout, because text movement could make an earlier accurate index wrong.

The finished list was shorter in some areas and richer in others. Its quality could not be measured simply by counting entries. It depended on anticipating reasonable questions and connecting them to the book's treatment of a subject.

The student had not altered the historical narrative. She had changed how readers could enter it. Preparing the index required an interpretation of topics and relationships, supported by testing with people who had not already learned the book's internal organisation.

questions.prompt: What weakness appeared in the first indexing method?
options: It contained no names at all.
It removed every page number.
It could miss substantial discussion using different words.
It replaced the book’s chapters with alphabetical order.
questions.explanation: C逐词搜漏以公司名讨论渡船的内容；A有姓名；B有页码；D正文未改。

questions.prompt: How did an index differ from the table of contents?
options: It offered topical routes across the chapter sequence.
It had to copy every chapter heading exactly.
It could contain only words printed on a cover.
It recorded when the book was purchased.
questions.explanation: A跨章按主题进入；B不是复制目录；C不局限封面；D非购买记录。

questions.prompt: Why add a cross-reference between company names?
options: To suggest two names always meant two unrelated subjects.
To remove the topic from the book.
To avoid all discussion of company history.
To help readers connect labels for the same subject.
questions.explanation: D跨名称连同主题；A反目的；B仍在书中；C不删历史。

questions.prompt: Why check numbers after final layout?
options: Readers were required to memorise earlier drafts.
Text movement could make earlier page references inaccurate.
The index had no relation to printed pages.
The chapter titles had to become longer.
questions.explanation: B排版后页变；A非读者记忆任务；C恰对应页；D非章节名长度。

questions.prompt: What made the completed index useful?
options: The largest possible number of entries regardless of meaning.
Its ability to replace reading every historical source.
Interpretation of topics combined with testing of readers’ likely questions.
An assumption that the book’s organisation was already known to everyone.
questions.explanation: C主题判断和真实查询测试；A数量非唯一；B索引不替研究；D测试陌生读者。

materials.title: A Tree Label for More than One Month
materials.text:
A college planted a trail of labelled trees for visitors. Each label included a photograph taken during spring flowering. In winter, several visitors could not match the photographs to the bare branches in front of them. One asked whether the trees had been replaced.

The trail designer had chosen the most colourful pictures rather than considering when people would visit. The photographs were accurate records of one season, but they did not supply every feature needed for recognition throughout the year.

The gardener suggested including smaller images of leaves, fruit and winter branches. A short description drew attention to bark and branch arrangement. These features did not all appear equally clearly at every time, so the label indicated which season each image showed. It also distinguished the tree's species name from the name of the person who had donated that particular tree.

The designer resisted turning each sign into a crowded textbook page. Visitors needed an entry point for observation, not a complete botanical manual. The team tested a simple arrangement with a large general image, a few seasonal details and a link to further information.

A local school then used the trail for repeated visits. Pupils noticed that recognising the same tree in different months required attending to different features. The label became a guide for comparison rather than a substitute for looking at the actual organism.

Some trees had similar leaves, so the team avoided suggesting that one isolated feature always settled identification. The signs presented a combination of clues and invited visitors to compare them. Where a cultivar name was known, that information was recorded separately from the broader species.

The revised trail did not make winter trees look like spring trees. It helped visitors understand the relationship between changing appearances. An accurate photograph could still be an incomplete guide when its conditions were hidden. Making season visible allowed the image to support observation instead of confusing a difference in time with a change in identity.

questions.prompt: Why did winter visitors struggle with the original labels?
options: The photographs depicted spring flowering rather than winter form.
All the trees had been secretly removed.
The images showed no real trees.
Visitors were asked to identify trees only from donor names.
questions.explanation: A照片季节差，冬枝不匹配；B未换树；C真实春照；D原本有植物图。

questions.prompt: What was added to improve recognition?
options: A rule that everyone should visit only in spring.
A claim that leaves never changed.
Seasonal details and descriptions of other visible features.
An identical photograph on every tree.
questions.explanation: C叶果冬枝及树皮枝序；A仍全年；B承认变；D非所有同照。

questions.prompt: Why did the designer limit the amount of information on each sign?
options: The species names were unavailable.
The sign should guide observation without becoming overcrowded.
Further information had to be permanently hidden.
Botanical features were irrelevant to recognition.
questions.explanation: B入口清楚不塞教材；A有种名；C有链接；D特征重要。

questions.prompt: What did repeated school visits reveal?
options: A tree could be identified only while flowering.
Every species had a unique leaf shape.
Donor names determined seasonal growth.
Different features could help recognise the same tree at different times.
questions.explanation: D同树不同季看不同线索；A冬也可；B相似叶需组合；C捐者不决定季变。

questions.prompt: What distinction is central to the passage?
options: All seasonal photographs are inaccurate.
A change of appearance over time need not mean a change of identity.
More information always makes a sign easier to use.
One leaf is sufficient to identify every tree.
questions.explanation: B时间外观异非换身份；A春照准确但不完整；C需克制；D单特征不必足够。

units.title: 六级阅读：共有牧场的规则与网页快照的边界
units.instruction: Read both complete passages and choose the best answer to each question using the passage it accompanies.

materials.title: A Common Field Was Not an Unruled Field
materials.text:
A policy workshop examined a fictional grazing area used by several villages. The land was described as common, and one participant inferred that anyone could bring any number of animals at any time. The local agreement described a different arrangement: recognised households held use rights subject to seasonal limits, monitoring and procedures for resolving disputes.

The case distinguished a resource shared under rules from a resource open to unrestricted entry. That distinction did not establish that the village system was fair or effective. Some households had little influence over rule-making, and new residents found access difficult. Understanding how the arrangement operated was a prerequisite for evaluating it, not an endorsement of every boundary it maintained.

Environmental variation complicated the seasonal limits. A fixed animal allowance that seemed reasonable after a wet winter could place greater pressure on pasture after drought. The agreement therefore allowed an announced review using observations of forage conditions. Users wanted discretion to respond to change, but they also wanted protection against arbitrary restrictions imposed after they had made costly plans.

Monitoring presented a similar tension. Villagers knew local conditions and could notice departures from the rules. Yet relying entirely on personal observation could expose less powerful households to selective enforcement. Written records and opportunities to challenge decisions gave local knowledge a more accountable role; they did not replace it with a view from nowhere.

A proposed reform would have granted individual plots to remove disputes over shared use. Some participants favoured the clarity of separate boundaries. Others noted that seasonal movement across the whole area helped households respond to uneven forage and water availability. Dividing the land could simplify one kind of responsibility while reducing another kind of flexibility.

The workshop did not declare common or individual arrangements universally superior. It compared who could use the resource, which decisions could change, how information entered those decisions and who could question enforcement. The relevant unit of analysis was a working set of rights and responsibilities, not the word common printed on a map.

The example suggests that institutional labels can hide substantial variation. A serious comparison must examine actual rules, distributions of voice and the conditions under which adaptation occurs. Shared use is not synonymous with absence of governance, and governance is not sufficient evidence of fairness. Keeping those propositions separate makes criticism more precise.

questions.prompt: What did the initial inference misunderstand?
options: Common use under an agreement need not mean unrestricted entry.
The villages had no animals.
Seasonal limits were physically impossible.
A map itself assigned every household equal influence.
questions.explanation: A共有有规则非无条件开放；B有牲畜；C可定限；D地图标签不保权力均等。

questions.prompt: Why did describing the agreement not endorse it?
options: Its written rules guaranteed equal participation.
The workshop was forbidden to discuss fairness.
Exclusion and unequal influence still required evaluation.
Every local decision was automatically effective.
questions.explanation: C理解运作仍需审权力排斥；A不保证；B正可评价；D非自动有效。

questions.prompt: What tension arose in adapting seasonal limits?
options: All users demanded permanently fixed weather.
Flexibility for environmental change had to coexist with protection from arbitrary decisions.
Drought removed every need for observation.
Announced review made planning irrelevant.
questions.explanation: B适应与可预期程序并重；A非控制天候；C旱更需观察；D用户已有成本计划。

questions.prompt: Why were written records and challenges added?
options: To prove local observers had no knowledge.
To eliminate every dispute by definition.
To prevent anyone from inspecting the pasture.
To make the use of local knowledge and enforcement more accountable.
questions.explanation: D约束选择执法并保留知识；A不否定本地经验；B不保无争；C仍监测。

questions.prompt: What qualification accompanied individual plots?
options: They might clarify boundaries while reducing useful movement flexibility.
They necessarily preserved all advantages of shared use.
They were rejected without discussion.
They made water and forage identical across the region.
questions.explanation: A产权清晰可能损流动适应；B有取舍；C讨论支持异议；D环境仍不均。

materials.title: The Page Saved without Its Conversation
materials.text:
A digital archive captured the homepage of a public discussion site on a particular date. The resulting image showed headlines, a list of recent comments and a banner inviting contributions. A researcher initially treated the capture as a complete record of what every visitor had encountered that day.

The archivist described several limits. The site personalised some content according to prior activity, and comment order could change as new responses arrived. The captured page was a record of one delivered state under particular conditions. Its timestamp was important, but a date alone did not identify every view available during that date.

Links added another complication. A visible headline might point to a page that had not been captured, while a preserved link destination could represent a different moment. A collection of saved pages was not automatically a complete reconstruction of a functioning site. Forms, searches and live updates could depend on services outside the archived material.

These limits did not make the archive worthless. The snapshot could provide evidence of wording, design and a particular ordering of visible material. It could also document that an invitation to participate had appeared. It could not, by itself, establish how many people saw the invitation or whether they were able to submit a response successfully.

The researcher consequently combined the capture with the archive's technical notes and other records. Where the required interaction had not survived, she marked the question unresolved. She avoided filling the gap with what a present version of the site happened to do, since later behaviour could reflect redesign rather than the earlier arrangement.

The archive improved its catalogue by specifying capture conditions and known missing functions. It also distinguished screenshots from preserved files that allowed some navigation. Both could be useful, but their differences affected the questions a user could investigate.

The episode illustrates why preservation of an interface should not be confused with preservation of every relation that once operated through it. A credible account identifies the state captured, the route by which it was obtained and the absent dependencies that constrain interpretation. The snapshot remains evidence, provided that its apparent completeness does not conceal the conditions that made it one particular view.

questions.prompt: Why was one dated capture not every visitor’s experience?
options: The archive had intentionally invented all headlines.
Personalisation and changing comment order could produce different delivered states.
The site had never permitted public access.
A timestamp made the image independent of its capture conditions.
questions.explanation: B个性化及动态顺序产生不同视图；A未伪造；C公开站；D时间戳不能替全部条件。

questions.prompt: What problem could linked pages create?
options: Every link necessarily led to a page from the same second.
All preserved links restored live services.
Headlines could not be evidence of wording.
Destinations might be missing or captured at different times.
questions.explanation: D目标缺失或不同时间；A不保证同秒；B动态服务可缺；C文字仍证据。

questions.prompt: What could the visible invitation alone support?
options: That the invitation appeared in the captured state.
That every visitor saw it.
That every attempted contribution succeeded.
That the number of participants equalled the comment count.
questions.explanation: A仅此状态出现邀请；B不能推所有人；C不能证提交成功；D未给参与人数等式。

questions.prompt: Why not use the current site to fill an earlier functional gap?
options: Present sites cannot be inspected at all.
Earlier interfaces never change.
Redesign could have changed the relevant behaviour.
Current behaviour automatically invalidates all old screenshots.
questions.explanation: C新版可能改功能；A可看但不作旧证；B会改；D不使老图全无效。

questions.prompt: What is the central requirement for credible use of the snapshot?
options: Treating an interface image as the full social interaction.
Keeping capture conditions and missing dependencies visible in interpretation.
Rejecting every digital archive as incomplete.
Assuming all saved files provide identical navigation.
questions.explanation: B解释条件和缺失依赖；A不是全关系；C资料仍有用；D截屏与可导航文件不同。

units.instruction: Read both complete passages and choose the best answer to each question using the passage it accompanies.

materials.title: Running the Script Was the Beginning
materials.text:
A research group released the code used to analyse a dataset and invited others to reproduce its result. A second team ran the script successfully and obtained the same numerical output. A news summary described the exercise as independent confirmation of the scientific claim.

The second team's report was more limited. The script used the same data, transformations and modelling assumptions as the original analysis. Obtaining the same output showed that the supplied computational procedure could be executed as described in the tested environment. It did not provide a new observation of the phenomenon or examine whether the original measurements supported the intended interpretation.

The distinction mattered when the team inspected a data-cleaning rule. It excluded records with a certain missing field. The code implemented that rule correctly, but the justification for exclusion was a substantive choice. A perfectly repeatable transformation could still remove a group whose absence affected the conclusion.

The team therefore separated several tasks. It verified execution, reconstructed the decisions that produced the analytic dataset and explored how reasonable alternative decisions affected the result. A further study with new observations would address another question. These tasks were related, but labelling all of them replication concealed what evidence each supplied.

Documentation proved crucial. A short comment explained why a category had been combined with another. Without that note, a later analyst could reproduce the operation but misunderstand its purpose. Reconstructing a decision required more than knowing the exact instruction passed to the computer.

The authors welcomed the report and corrected an overbroad claim in their release announcement. They did not withdraw the code or portray repeatability as unimportant. Computational access allowed other researchers to identify and question choices that a final table alone would conceal.

The case supports a layered account of verification. Matching output is a valuable achievement, especially when complicated workflows are otherwise inaccessible. Its evidential force depends on what has been held fixed and what has been tested independently. A claim about reliable execution, a claim about the robustness of analytical choices and a claim about a phenomenon need not rise or fall together. Clear description allows each to receive the scrutiny appropriate to it.

questions.prompt: What did matching the output establish directly?
options: A new measurement of the phenomenon.
That all data exclusions were substantively justified.
Successful execution of the supplied procedure in the tested environment.
Independent validation of every modelling assumption.
questions.explanation: C直接证可执行且同结果；A没新观测；B、D合理性尚未独立检验。

questions.prompt: Why inspect the exclusion rule despite correct code?
options: A correctly executed choice could still affect the substantive interpretation.
Correct implementation made all records identical.
The rule could not be read by anyone.
Missing fields automatically justified excluding every affected group.
questions.explanation: A规则对但排除对象影响结论；B数据异；C代码可查；D缺项非自动充分理由。

questions.prompt: Why distinguish verification tasks?
options: To ensure no one could question the result.
To claim all tasks supplied identical evidence.
To replace new observations with documentation alone.
To identify what each procedure tested and what it held fixed.
questions.explanation: D分清各层证据；A促进质疑；B不等同；C新研究另解问题。

questions.prompt: What did the explanatory comment contribute?
options: It made alternative analyses unnecessary.
It helped reconstruct the purpose behind a transformation.
It proved the chosen category was the only conceivable one.
It changed the computer’s arithmetic without changing code.
questions.explanation: B解释操作意图；A仍可敏感性分析；C不证唯一；D注释不是算法改动。

questions.prompt: How does the passage value released code?
options: It is useful only if it confirms the claim completely.
It can enable meaningful scrutiny even though repeatable output is not full scientific confirmation.
It is less informative than hiding all methods.
It eliminates the distinction between data and assumptions.
questions.explanation: B代码助复核但不等全证实；A有限证据也有用；C开放更可审；D仍分数据假设。

materials.title: The Empty Chair at the Consultation
materials.text:
A transport authority invited residents to discuss a proposed route change. Its report stated that the public had been consulted because an evening meeting had been held and written comments accepted for two weeks. The participation officer asked whether those procedural facts captured the quality of the opportunity offered.

The meeting had taken place in an accessible building, but its evening time conflicted with some shift workers' schedules. The written form asked users to respond to a detailed map that assumed familiarity with current route numbers. A legal opportunity to submit a comment did not ensure that every affected person could understand the proposal or take advantage of the channel.

The officer did not infer that every absent person opposed the plan. Absence could have several causes, including satisfaction, lack of information or practical barriers. The same empty chair could not reveal which reason applied. Nor could the authority treat silence as approval merely because it had offered one route to participation.

Additional outreach used short descriptions of the journeys affected and sessions at different times. Staff recorded which groups remained difficult to reach. They did not claim that speaking to a representative automatically reproduced all the experiences within a group.

The authority also clarified the scope of influence. Some constraints, such as a funding limit, were already fixed. Other choices remained open. Presenting a settled decision as negotiable would invite effort under a false expectation. Conversely, using a fixed budget to imply that every design detail was beyond discussion would hide real choices.

After considering responses, the authority published a reasoned account of changes and retained decisions. Consultation did not promise that every preference would prevail. It created an obligation to listen within an honestly described process and explain how relevant contributions affected the outcome.

The revised evaluation distinguished an event having occurred from participation having been meaningfully enabled. Counting submissions remained useful, but it could not settle whose experiences were missing or whether participants understood what they could influence. The case makes a procedural claim more demanding without making unanimous agreement its standard: a consultation can be criticised for its design even when no conclusion is available about what every absent resident would have wanted.

questions.prompt: What limit did the officer identify in the authority’s initial claim?
options: Holding a meeting did not by itself demonstrate the quality of participation opportunities.
Written comments were impossible by definition.
Every absent resident had submitted an objection.
An accessible building guaranteed equal practical access to the process.
questions.explanation: A程序发生不等机会充分；B可书面；C不能推缺席都反；D时间理解仍有障碍。

questions.prompt: How should absence be interpreted?
options: As evidence of unanimous support.
As evidence of unanimous opposition.
As potentially arising from different causes that require investigation.
As proof that the route affected nobody.
questions.explanation: C缺席多因不能单解；A、B极端推断；D有人受影响。

questions.prompt: Why clarify fixed and open decisions?
options: To promise every participant their preferred outcome.
To describe honestly what participation could influence.
To avoid publishing any proposal.
To remove all design choices whenever funding was limited.
questions.explanation: B不虚诺可改范围；A非人人如愿；C仍公开；D预算定不等细节全定。

questions.prompt: What did the authority owe participants after considering comments?
options: Automatic adoption of the most frequent phrase.
A guarantee that no resident remained dissatisfied.
A private report available only to planners.
An explanation of changes and reasons for retained decisions.
questions.explanation: D合理反馈改变与保留缘由；A不是词频投票；B不保满意；C公开说明。

questions.prompt: Which standard does the passage support?
options: Unanimity is required before consultation can occur.
Submission counts prove that all experiences were represented.
Participation must be meaningfully enabled without treating silence as a known preference.
Every fixed constraint makes consultation dishonest.
questions.explanation: C设计可参与且不伪推静默态度；A不以一致为标准；B数量不能证代表；D诚实说明约束仍可咨询。

units.instruction: Read both complete passages and choose the best answer to each question using the passage it accompanies.

materials.title: A Larger Menu of Courses
materials.text:
A university proposed replacing several required modules with a broad elective menu. Advocates described the change as an increase in student choice. In one sense the description was accurate: the catalogue would contain more combinations from which an individual could select. The curriculum committee nevertheless asked what conditions made those combinations usable.

Some modules shared prerequisites, and several ran at the same time. A student could not necessarily assemble the programme suggested by a list of independent course titles. Access also depended on capacity. An attractive elective with a small enrolment limit might be nominally available while remaining inaccessible to many students.

Advising introduced a less visible difference. Students with family members familiar with university study often arrived with ideas about coherent combinations and future requirements. Others had to infer the implications from brief descriptions. Removing requirements could transfer the work of building a coherent path from the institution to the student, with unequal support for performing that work.

The committee did not conclude that compulsory modules were inherently fairer. Requirements could preserve outdated priorities or prevent students pursuing valuable interests. The issue was how much coordination the institution supplied, how clearly it explained dependencies and which possibilities a student could realistically reach.

A revised proposal retained several shared foundations while creating clusters of electives with published pathways and space for individual alternatives. Staff tested sample timetables and expanded advice at decision points. The pathways were examples, not undisclosed compulsory sequences. Students could see why certain combinations prepared them for particular later work.

Evaluation would consider more than how many elective titles appeared in the catalogue. The committee planned to examine actual access, reasons for rejected choices and students' understanding of consequences. A student declining a course by preference was different from one abandoning it because a required prerequisite had been unavailable.

The proposal thus treated choice as a relationship between options and the means to use them. Increasing the menu could be valuable, but the menu's length did not exhaust the question. An institution supporting autonomy needed to make conditions, dependencies and sources of advice visible, rather than assuming that formal permission alone placed every student in an equivalent position.

questions.prompt: Why was the larger catalogue an incomplete measure of choice?
options: It contained no genuinely different subjects.
Prerequisites, scheduling and capacity affected which combinations could be used.
Every student had identical prior knowledge.
Electives could never contribute to a coherent degree.
questions.explanation: B依赖时间容量限制实际可选；A有更多组合；C支援背景不同；D可形成合理路径。

questions.prompt: What inequality could removing requirements expose?
options: All compulsory courses had previously been free of outdated assumptions.
Only students with relatives at university could enrol.
The university would lose the ability to publish descriptions.
Students differed in support for constructing an informed coherent path.
questions.explanation: D规划支持不同；A未说旧要求全合理；B非资格限制；C仍可描述。

questions.prompt: How did the committee regard compulsory modules?
options: They could help coordination but also preserve outdated priorities.
They were always the fairest arrangement.
They made advising useless.
They prevented any meaningful comparison of curricula.
questions.explanation: A协调有益亦可过时；B不绝对；C仍需建议；D可以比较。

questions.prompt: What role did the published pathways serve?
options: They concealed a mandatory sequence.
They guaranteed a place in every class.
They explained useful combinations while preserving alternatives.
They eliminated the need to consider timetables.
questions.explanation: C示范依赖用途并允许别路径；A非隐性强制；B未保席位；D实际测试课表。

questions.prompt: What distinction would the evaluation examine?
options: The font size of all course titles.
A choice declined through preference versus one blocked by unavailable prerequisites.
Whether every student selected the same cluster.
Whether a longer catalogue always increased autonomy.
questions.explanation: B偏好不选与结构被堵不同；A非字形；C不要求同选；D要检验而非假定必增自主。

materials.title: What the Night Shift Needed to Know
materials.text:
A maintenance team responsible for a large public building kept a detailed manual of equipment and procedures. When two experienced workers retired, managers assumed that the manual preserved everything the replacement staff would need. Early shifts revealed a different picture.

The manual described normal operation clearly, but the retiring workers had also learned patterns through repeated observation. One knew that a particular vibration often followed a recent adjustment; another recognised which reported fault usually originated in a nearby unit. This knowledge was not supernatural intuition. It connected observations across time, locations and previous interventions.

Managers first proposed recording every memory as another manual entry. The workers helped, but a list of isolated tips created problems. Some observations were conditional on equipment later replaced. Others described a clue to investigate rather than a reliable diagnosis. Without context, a useful suspicion could be mistaken for a rule.

The team therefore combined documentation with supervised shifts. New workers followed the route from a report to an inspection and discussed why one observation changed the next question. Records linked a suspected pattern to the checks that could confirm or challenge it. The aim was not to turn individual anecdotes into unquestionable instructions.

The handover also exposed distributed knowledge. A cleaner noticed leaks early; a receptionist could identify when unusual noises were reported; maintenance staff understood the machinery. No one person held the complete operational picture. A process for sharing observations mattered as much as collecting the memories of senior technicians.

The resulting system retained the manual, added contextual records and protected time for discussion between shifts. It also established routes for escalating uncertainty rather than encouraging replacements to imitate confidence. A successful handover meant that future staff could reason and learn, not merely repeat the last employee's conclusions.

The case qualifies the idea that organisational knowledge is captured once its documents have been copied. Documentation is essential, but its usefulness depends on interpretation, relevance and the connections among people who observe different parts of a process. Preserving expertise can require maintaining those relationships and practices as well as storing statements. The retirement problem was partly about lost experience and partly about whether the organisation had created ways for experience to become shareable evidence.

questions.prompt: What did early replacement shifts reveal?
options: The manual covered normal operation but not all contextual patterns known by workers.
Experienced workers had never used evidence.
No equipment in the building had written instructions.
Retirement had made every machine physically different.
questions.explanation: A手册正常流程清晰但漏累积关联；B经验来自观察；C有手册；D非设备全变。

questions.prompt: Why could isolated tips be misleading?
options: All past observations were invented.
Every clue was a definite diagnosis.
Their conditions or status as tentative clues could be lost.
Written notes could not contain dates.
questions.explanation: C条件变化或线索非定论需上下文；A非捏造；B正需辨；D可记日期。

questions.prompt: What did supervised shifts add?
options: A rule against asking experienced staff questions.
Practice tracing observations into testable questions and checks.
A guarantee that new staff would never face uncertainty.
A replacement for all equipment records.
questions.explanation: B学查证推理路径；A可讨论；C不保零不确定；D仍留手册。

questions.prompt: What did distributed knowledge imply?
options: Only technicians could report useful facts.
The receptionist should diagnose every machine alone.
Copying one person’s memories captured the whole building.
A process connecting different observers was important.
questions.explanation: D清洁前台技术各见一环需连结；A多角色均有用；B不是前台单诊；C无人全知。

questions.prompt: What characterised a successful handover?
options: The permanent removal of uncertainty from maintenance.
The ability to reason and learn using records and shared practices.
Memorising every retired worker’s conclusion as a rule.
Replacing all documentation with informal conversations.
questions.explanation: B资料与协作维持学习推理；A仍不确定；C不盲照结论；D文件仍重要。

units.instruction: Read both complete passages and choose the best answer to each question using the passage it accompanies.

materials.title: The Word That Changed the Claim
materials.text:
An editor preparing a public summary of a research report replaced the phrase consistent with an association with shows that one factor causes another. The new sentence was shorter and more direct. It also asserted a relationship the original report had not established.

The researchers had observed a pattern in records collected for another purpose. They discussed alternative explanations, including differences between the groups that existed before the measured exposure. Their cautious wording did not merely express a lack of confidence in their arithmetic. It identified a limit on what the study design could distinguish.

The editor initially proposed restoring uncertainty by adding probably to the causal sentence. A methods adviser explained that this would not recover the original meaning. The problem was not only the degree of confidence attached to a fixed claim; the kind of relationship being claimed had changed. A tentative causal statement remained a causal statement.

A revised summary described the observed association and briefly identified the design limitation. It then reported why the result mattered and what further evidence could help assess the proposed explanation. This was longer than the original headline, but it connected significance with an honest account of evidential strength.

The team did not insist on copying every technical qualifier. Some phrases existed to satisfy conventions familiar to specialist readers and could be explained more clearly in ordinary language. The task was to preserve the distinctions doing substantive work, rather than retain all the original vocabulary or remove all of it.

The discussion also covered the word significant. In the report it referred to a specified statistical calculation, not necessarily a large or practically important effect. The public summary therefore gave an interpretable description of the result's scale instead of relying on that word to convey importance.

The episode shows that translating research for a wider audience requires decisions about claims, not just sentence length. Clarity can improve understanding when it makes the relevant distinctions easier to grasp. It becomes misleading when it achieves confidence by deleting the limits that determine what a result means. A useful summary allows readers to see both why the finding deserves attention and which conclusions remain beyond the supplied evidence.

questions.prompt: Why did the first edit change the report’s meaning?
options: It used fewer words but preserved every relationship.
It reported a larger sample than the study contained.
It changed an observed association into a causal claim.
It replaced the observed groups with a new experiment.
questions.explanation: C将关联升因果；A没保核心关系；B未改样本数；D研究未变只是报道变。

questions.prompt: What did the original caution identify?
options: A design limit on distinguishing explanations.
An inability to perform any arithmetic.
A claim that the observed pattern did not exist.
A requirement that public readers learn every technical convention.
questions.explanation: A设计不能区分替代解释；B不是算术无能；C观察到模式；D可用普通语言。

questions.prompt: Why was probably insufficient?
options: It made the sentence grammatically impossible.
It guaranteed the claim was false.
It removed every uncertainty from the statement.
It changed confidence without restoring the original kind of claim.
questions.explanation: D弱化置信但仍因果；A语法可；B未判必假；C有不确定但类别仍错。

questions.prompt: How did the revised summary handle technical language?
options: It copied every qualifier without explanation.
It preserved substantive distinctions while explaining them accessibly.
It removed all design information.
It used statistical significance as the sole measure of practical importance.
questions.explanation: B保实质区分并易懂表达；A不机械全抄；C加设计限；D给规模避免混意义。

questions.prompt: Which view of clarity is supported?
options: A confident sentence is necessarily the most accurate.
Clarity depends partly on retaining the limits that define the claim.
Any longer summary is automatically more reliable.
Research can be translated without interpreting its claims.
questions.explanation: B界限决定意思也是清晰内容；A自信非准确；C非长度自动；D需要判断主张。

materials.title: A Gift with a Place on the Shelf
materials.text:
A private collector offered a university library a substantial set of books on regional crafts. The gift would fill recognised gaps in the collection. It also came with a condition: the books had to remain permanently together under the donor's family name, with no item removed from the group.

The librarian welcomed the subject coverage but examined the long-term implications. Some volumes duplicated existing holdings, while others required conservation. Space, cataloguing and care would impose continuing costs even though the purchase price was zero. Calling the collection free obscured the distinction between acquisition payment and stewardship.

Keeping the books together could serve a legitimate purpose. The collector's arrangement showed relationships among trades and regions, and researchers might value that intellectual history. Yet a permanent physical grouping could make individual volumes harder to use alongside related material elsewhere in the library. Preserving information about an arrangement did not always require preserving its precise shelf location indefinitely.

The librarian proposed documenting the original order in the catalogue and retaining links identifying the collection. The library would then be able to relocate items for care or use, while keeping the provenance visible. The donor worried that dispersion would erase the family association, so the partners discussed how recognition could survive changes in storage.

A further issue concerned future withdrawals. No institution could know every conservation problem or collecting priority that would emerge decades later. Accepting an absolute prohibition might require keeping unusable duplicates or prevent a responsible transfer. The librarian sought a review process rather than promising an inflexible rule the institution might later be unable to honour.

The final agreement preserved the collection's identity and history while permitting documented professional decisions about location and retention. It did not give the library unrestricted permission to disregard the donor's concerns. It made the purposes of recognition, research access and continuing care explicit enough to negotiate.

The gift became valuable through an arrangement that acknowledged both its benefits and obligations. The case illustrates how a generous offer can create future commitments requiring scrutiny. Responsible acceptance involves explaining how an institution will sustain access and meaning over time, rather than assuming that gratitude requires every condition to remain untouched forever.

questions.prompt: What did the librarian question about calling the gift free?
options: The books had no possible research value.
Ongoing storage, care and cataloguing still required resources.
The donor secretly demanded a purchase price.
All duplicate books were legally worthless.
